title: Isaiah
subtitle: The Holy One of Israel, judgment and comfort for Zion
lead: Isaiah has more chapters than any other prophet, and it is the prophet the New Testament quotes most. It opens as "the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz" about Judah and Jerusalem, seen in the days of four kings of Judah: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1). Those reigns cover the second half of the 700s BC, when the Assyrian empire swallowed the small kingdoms of the west. Isaiah watched Assyria destroy the northern kingdom of Israel (722 BC) and then overrun Judah and surround Jerusalem (701 BC). He spoke to kings at the water conduit and in the palace, to the leaders and the wealthy women of Jerusalem, and to the crowds at the Temple.

The book's center is a vision. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, and heard the seraphim call to one another, "Holy, holy, holy" (6:3). His name for God throughout the book is "the Holy One of Israel", a title found twenty-five times in Isaiah and only a handful of times in the rest of the Bible. Because the LORD is holy, the book says, injustice in Jerusalem cannot stand: the city will be judged, purged and left with a remnant. Because the LORD is also faithful to Zion, judgment is not the last word: Jerusalem will be rebuilt, the exiles will come home in a new exodus, the nations will stream to the LORD's mountain, and in the end there will be new heavens and a new earth.

From chapter 40 on, the book speaks to a people who have lost everything: "Comfort, comfort my people" (40:1). Babylon has replaced Assyria, the Temple lies in ruins, and the exiles wonder whether God has forgotten them. These chapters name Cyrus of Persia as the LORD's chosen deliverer (44:28; 45:1) and introduce the LORD's servant, who suffers for others (52:13–53:12). How these chapters relate to the prophet of the 700s is the book's great question of authorship, and this site gives the main answers side by side. Jews read Isaiah's comfort in the synagogue in the seven weeks after the fast of the Ninth of Av; Christians, from the Gospels on, read it as the prophecy of Jesus, so often that Jerome said Isaiah should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet.
facts: The book is headed "the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz" (1:1), and his name, Yesha'yahu, means "the LORD saves". He lived in Jerusalem, was married to a woman he calls "the prophetess" (8:3), and had at least two sons whose names were signs (7:3; 8:3). Jewish and Christian tradition holds that he wrote the whole book. Most modern scholars assign much of 1–39 to him and 40–66 to later prophets who carried on his teaching (see the authorship section).

Isaiah was active from about 740 BC, the year King Uzziah died (6:1), to at least 701 BC, when Sennacherib of Assyria besieged Jerusalem (36–37). Jewish and Christian tradition says he was put to death under Manasseh, after about 687 BC (697 if Manasseh first ruled with his father). Dates for the kings follow Edwin Thiele's system, as elsewhere on this site; other systems differ by up to about twenty years. Scholars who date 40–55 to the exile place it around 550–539 BC, and 56–66 after the return of 538 BC. The whole book existed by about 180 BC, when Ben Sira praised Isaiah (Sirach 48:22–25), and a complete copy survives from about 125 BC.

Jerusalem and Judah under the Davidic kings, in the shadow of Assyria, then Babylon, then Persia. Chapters 1–39 move between the Temple, the royal court and the streets of Jerusalem; chapters 40–55 address the exiles in Babylon, whether as prophecy written ahead of time or as preaching among them, and 56–66 address a community in Judah after the return, or, on the traditional view, Isaiah's own people looking ahead to it (see the audience views).

Prophecy: mostly oracles in Hebrew poetry (judgment speeches, woes, songs, laments, oracles against foreign nations, promises of salvation), with prose stories about the prophet (6–8; 20; 36–39) and Hezekiah's psalm (38:9–20). Chapters 24–27 are often called "the Isaiah Apocalypse".
Classical Hebrew of high literary quality, with many rare words, wordplays and sound-plays. The Greek translation, made in Egypt in the 100s BC, is free and often paraphrases.

The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran Cave 1 (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) contains all 66 chapters. It is the oldest complete book of the Hebrew Bible, about a thousand years older than the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), and it differs from it mostly in spelling. Another twenty copies from Qumran preserve parts of the book.

In Jewish Bibles it heads the Latter Prophets, followed by Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve (one Talmud passage places it after Jeremiah and Ezekiel, Bava Batra 14b). In Protestant Bibles it follows the Song of Songs as the first of the Major Prophets; in Catholic Bibles it follows Sirach; in Orthodox Bibles, which keep the order of the Greek Old Testament, it comes after the Twelve.
authorship: Jewish and Christian tradition holds that Isaiah son of Amoz wrote the whole book in the 700s and early 600s BC. Sirach, about 180 BC, praises Isaiah because 'by a powerful spirit he saw the last things, and comforted those who mourned in Zion' (Sirach 48:24), a reference to chapters 40–66, and the New Testament quotes both halves under his name (John 12:38–41 quotes 53:1 and 6:10 together; Romans 10:16–20 quotes 53:1 and 65:1). The Talmud's statement that 'Hezekiah and his company wrote Isaiah' (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a) is usually read as copying or editing, not composing. Defenders of a single author include E. J. Young and O. T. Allis and, more recently, J. A. Motyer and John Oswalt; among Jewish scholars, Rachel Margalioth argued the case in The Indivisible Isaiah (1964). They argue that predictive prophecy, including the naming of Cyrus (44:28; 45:1), is exactly what the book claims to offer (41:21–29; 46:9–10); that the vocabulary and theology of the two halves, above all 'the Holy One of Israel', are too close to be chance; that the scene of chapters 40–66 is not clearly Babylonian in its trees, idols and geography; and that no ancient witness shows a break between chapters 39 and 40: in the Great Isaiah Scroll, 40:1 begins on the last line of the column that ends chapter 39. (The scroll's one visible break, after 33:24, falls elsewhere.)

Most critical scholars since the late 1700s hold that the book grew over two centuries or more. Ibn Ezra, in the 1100s, hinted in his comment on 40:1 that the second half spoke of the exile from a later time, adding that 'the wise will understand'. Johann Christoph Döderlein (1775) and J. G. Eichhorn argued that chapters 40–66 come from an anonymous prophet of the exile, and Bernhard Duhm (1892) divided them into Second Isaiah (40–55), a prophet of the 540s BC (Duhm himself placed him in Phoenicia; most later scholars place him among the exiles in Babylon), and Third Isaiah (56–66), whom Duhm dated to the generation before Nehemiah; most scholars now think of several prophets in Judah after the return of 538. Duhm also set the servant songs apart as the work of another author. Their reasons: chapters 40–55 address exiles in Babylon as people already living there, call Jerusalem ruined and about to be rebuilt (44:26–28), and name Cyrus as a figure the hearers know (45:1–4); Isaiah of Jerusalem never appears in them; and the style, vocabulary and themes (creation, monotheism, the servant) differ from 1–39. Within 1–39, too, scholars assign some chapters (such as 13–14, 24–27 and 34–35) to later writers.

Since the 1970s many scholars, such as Brevard Childs, Rolf Rendtorff, Christopher Seitz, H. G. M. Williamson and Marvin Sweeney, have stressed that the book was edited to be read as one. Words and themes are threaded through the whole: 'the Holy One of Israel', 'Comfort', the highway, the remnant, Zion. Williamson argued that the writer of 40–55 knew and continued an early form of 1–39 and helped shape it; others see the final editing in the Persian period, when chapters 1 and 65–66 were set as the book's frame. On this view the book's unity lies not in one author but in one tradition: Isaiah's disciples, to whom he entrusted his teaching (8:16), and their heirs, who read the old prophecies as fulfilled and still to be fulfilled.

audience.to: Chapters 1–39 were first spoken to Judah and Jerusalem in the late 700s BC: to kings Ahaz and Hezekiah and their court, to the judges, priests and wealthy landowners of Jerusalem, to the people who crowded the Temple courts with sacrifices, and sometimes to the northern kingdom of Israel and to foreign nations, usually in Judah's hearing. Chapters 40–55 address Jews who have lost their land and Temple and live as exiles in Babylon, whether as prophecy written ahead of time or as preaching among them, and chapters 56–66 address a community in Judah after the return, divided over worship, justice and who may belong, or, on the traditional view, Isaiah's own people looking ahead to that time (see the views). The finished book was read by Jews of the Persian and Greek periods, in Judah and abroad, as one message to them.
audience.why: Isaiah of Jerusalem called a prosperous, religious and unjust city to turn back to the Holy One of Israel, to trust him instead of alliances with Assyria or Egypt, and to see the coming Assyrian invasions as his judgment; he also promised that a remnant would survive and that a righteous king of David's line would come. The later chapters answer despair: they tell exiles that the LORD has not forgotten Zion, that he controls history and will bring them home, and they tell the returned community what true worship and justice look like while it waits for the full restoration. Read together, the book teaches its readers to see their own day inside one story of judgment and renewal, from Jerusalem's sin (1) to the new heavens and the new earth (65–66).
views: One prophet, one audience in view

Many conservative Jewish and Christian scholars hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book. On this view chapters 40–66 were written in Hezekiah's reign or later in Isaiah's life for a generation not yet born, to be read by the exiles when Babylon's fall came; naming Cyrus long before his birth shows that the LORD alone knows the future, which is the argument of those chapters themselves (41:21–29; 44:24–28; 45:21) (Young; Oswalt; Motyer).

Most critical scholars since Döderlein (1775) and Duhm (1892) hear three audiences: Judah in the 700s (much of 1–39), exiles in Babylon around 550–539 BC addressed directly by an unnamed prophet ("Second Isaiah", 40–55), and Judeans after the return of 538 BC ("Third Isaiah", 56–66). On this view Cyrus is named because he was already on the march, and the comfort is for people living through the events (Blenkinsopp). Duhm himself placed Second Isaiah in Phoenicia and dated Third Isaiah to the generation before Nehemiah.

Many recent scholars, of both views, stress that whatever its origins, the book was edited to be read as a whole by Jews of the Persian period: its first chapter already looks forward to its last, and themes such as Zion, the Holy One of Israel and the highway of return bind the parts together (Childs; Williamson; Rendtorff; Sweeney).

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads each oracle against the events it names and asks what it meant for its first hearers: the Syro-Ephraimite war of 734 BC, Assyria's conquests of Samaria (722) and Judah (701), Babylon's fall to Cyrus (539) and the return. It traces how the events the prophet announced turned out.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made: most scholars assign chapters 1–39 largely to Isaiah of Jerusalem with later additions, 40–55 to a prophet of the exile (Second Isaiah) and 56–66 to prophets after the return (Third Isaiah), while recent work stresses how the whole was edited as one book. It also weighs the Great Isaiah Scroll, the Greek translation and the Assyrian and Babylonian records.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: How the Targum, the rabbis and the medieval commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, Abravanel) read Isaiah: the servant as Israel, the consolations read in synagogue after the Ninth of Av, and the hope of the messianic age and the return to Zion.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: How the New Testament, which quotes Isaiah more than any other book except the Psalms, and the church after it read the book as pointing to Jesus: Immanuel, the child of 9:6, the shoot of Jesse, the voice in the wilderness and the suffering servant. Jerome said Isaiah should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet; later Christians called the book 'the fifth gospel'.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads the promises of a world at peace, a restored Israel in its land and a new heaven and earth (2:2–4; 11:6–9; 65:17–25) as still waiting for their full fulfillment: in many Christian readings at Christ's return and a reign on earth (premillennial and dispensational), and in Jewish hope in the days of the Messiah.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Isaiah is among the most memorized books of the Bible, through Christmas and Good Friday readings and Handel's Messiah; the Plain keeps familiar wording only where the Hebrew forces it. Most of Isaiah is poetry: the Plain keeps one verse per line and marks the poetic lines with slashes. The prose chapters (parts of 6–8, 20 and 36–39) have no slashes. Where Isaiah plays on words, the Plain keeps the play if English can (5:7) and otherwise explains it in a note.

Key terms

YHWH is "the LORD"; Adonai YHWH is "the Lord GOD"; YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies"; qedosh Yisra'el is "the Holy One of Israel"; bat Tsiyyon is "Daughter Zion". Hoy is "Woe to", ne'um YHWH is "the LORD declares", massa' is "oracle" and koh amar YHWH is "The LORD says this". Mishpat and tsedaqah are "justice" and "righteousness"; torah is "teaching"; hesed is "loyal love"; 'elilim are "worthless idols"; she'ar is "remnant"; the servant of chapters 40–55 is written in lower case; She'ol is left as "Sheol"; go'el, used of God, is "redeemer"; and 'almah in 7:14 is "young woman" (see the note there).

Verse numbers

The Plain uses English verse numbers. They differ from the Hebrew in two places: English 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23, and English 9:2–21 is Hebrew 9:1–20; English 64:1 is the second half of Hebrew 63:19, and English 64:2–12 is Hebrew 64:1–11.

The text and the versions

The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex. The Great Isaiah Scroll and the other Qumran copies were read through the site's transcription of the scrolls, and the Greek through Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus, compared where it matters with Ziegler's critical text. Each chapter page says which witnesses were read for it. Readings that change the sense are given as variants.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible, the King James Version, the American Standard Version, Young's Literal Translation and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

Isaiah son of Amoz lived in Jerusalem in the second half of the 700s BC. He had access to kings (7:3; 37:21; 38:1), was married to a woman he calls 'the prophetess' (8:3) and gave his sons names that were messages (7:3; 8:3). His dated words run from the year Uzziah died, about 740 BC (6:1), to Sennacherib's invasion in 701 (36–37) and Hezekiah's last years.

Dates for the kings follow Edwin Thiele's system, used throughout this site (Uzziah died in 740/739 BC; Ahaz reigned about 735–715 and Hezekiah about 715–686); other systems, such as those of Hayes and Hooker or Galil, differ by up to about twenty years.

Those decades saw the rise of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Tiglath-pileser III (745–727) built a standing army and began yearly campaigns west. In 734–732 Aram and Israel tried to force Judah into a revolt; Ahaz instead asked Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7–8), and Assyria crushed Damascus and took Galilee. In 722 Samaria fell and the northern kingdom ended (2 Kings 17). Under Sargon II, Ashdod rebelled and was taken in 711 (20:1). In 705 Hezekiah joined a revolt with Egypt's support, against Isaiah's warnings (30–31), and in 701 Sennacherib took Judah's walled towns and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared (36–37; 2 Kings 18–19). Sennacherib's own annals and the reliefs of Lachish from his palace at Nineveh record the campaign.

Chapters 40–66 speak to a later world: Babylon is the great power, Jerusalem lies in ruins, and Cyrus of Persia, who took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles return, is named (44:28; 45:1). How these chapters relate to Isaiah of Jerusalem is discussed under authorship.

Isaiah falls into several large blocks:

  • 1–12: oracles about Judah and Jerusalem, with Isaiah's call (6) and the Immanuel chapters (7–12), ending in a song (12).
  • 13–23: oracles against the nations, from Babylon to Tyre.
  • 24–27: the judgment and renewal of the whole earth, often called the 'Isaiah Apocalypse'.
  • 28–35: woes on Samaria and Jerusalem for trusting Egypt, then the King in his beauty and the highway home (33–35).
  • 36–39: the stories of Hezekiah, also told in 2 Kings 18–20, ending with a warning of Babylon (39).
  • 40–55: comfort for exiles: the LORD the only God, Cyrus his instrument, the servant, and Zion restored.
  • 56–66: the community after the return: foreigners welcome, true and false worship, Zion's glory, and new heavens and a new earth.

Chapters 36–39 form a hinge: they close the Assyrian story and open the Babylonian one. Chapters 1 and 65–66 frame the book with the same words: heaven and earth, rebels, gardens, Sabbaths and unquenchable fire.

The Holy One of Israel. Isaiah's name for God appears about 25 times in the book, in both halves, and only a handful of times elsewhere. It comes from the vision of 6:3: the God whose holiness fills the earth has bound himself to Israel. Zion. Jerusalem is the city judged (1; 3; 29), spared (37), mourned (40; 51) and rebuilt as the center of the world (2:2–4; 60–62). The remnant. Judgment leaves a few, a 'holy seed' (6:13), from whom a people will grow (10:20–22; 37:31–32). Justice and righteousness. What God looked for in his vineyard (5:7) and what the coming king will bring (9:7; 11:4; 32:1). The king and the servant. A child on David's throne (9:6–7; 11:1–10) and a servant who suffers for many (52:13–53:12). The new exodus. A road through the desert, water in dry land, and the exiles brought home (35; 40:3–5; 43:16–21; 52:11–12). The new creation. The God who made the heavens will make new heavens and a new earth (65:17; 66:22).

sections.h: The Great Isaiah Scroll and the other Qumran copies
sections.b:
The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) was found in 1947 in Cave 1 at Qumran, by the Dead Sea. It is the only biblical book from Qumran that survives complete: 54 columns on 17 sheets of leather sewn together, about 7.3 meters (24 feet) long, copied about 125 BC. It is kept in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem. A second copy from the same cave (1QIsa-b) preserves parts of many chapters, most of them in the second half of the book, and Cave 4 yielded parts of at least eighteen more, with one more from Cave 5 and a fragment from Wadi Murabba'at: more copies than of any other prophet.

The Great Isaiah Scroll agrees with the Masoretic Text, copied over a thousand years later, in the vast majority of its words. Most of its differences are spelling: it writes many more vowel letters and some Aramaic-influenced forms (Kutscher). Some readings change the sense, such as the two 'holies' of 6:3, the gap at 2:9b–10, 'light' in 53:11 and 'he will call' in 7:14; these are given as variants. The scroll leaves a gap of three lines at the end of chapter 33, and its second half, from chapter 34, was copied by a different scribe, which some have taken as evidence that the book was once handled in two halves.

Isaiah was translated into Greek in Egypt, probably in Alexandria, in the second century BC. The translator worked freely: he often paraphrased, smoothed hard lines, and sometimes read his own times into the text, as Seeligmann showed (Seeligmann). On this site 'the Greek' means the critical text of Ziegler's Göttingen edition (1939) or Rahlfs; Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus, is the one this site's tools display, and readings found only there are named by that codex.

The Greek matters because the New Testament often quotes Isaiah in its words: 6:9–10 ('their heart has grown fat'), 7:14 (parthenos, 'virgin'), 40:3–8, 42:1–4, 53:1 and 53:7–8, among many others. Where it does, the note on the verse says so.

sections.h: Isaiah in the New Testament and the church
sections.b:
The New Testament quotes Isaiah by name more often than any other prophet, about twenty times, and alludes to it far more. The Gospels open with the voice in the wilderness (40:3; Mark 1:2–3); Jesus begins his preaching in Nazareth by reading 61:1–2 (Luke 4:16–21); Philip explains 53:7–8 to an Ethiopian official (Acts 8:30–35); Paul builds his argument about Israel and the nations in Romans 9–11 largely from Isaiah. Matthew sees Immanuel (7:14), the light in Galilee (9:1–2) and the servant (42:1–4) fulfilled in Jesus.

Jerome wrote that Isaiah 'should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet', and later Christians called the book 'the fifth gospel' (Sawyer). Its words fill the Advent and Christmas readings (7:14; 9:2–7; 11:1–10; 40:1–11), the Good Friday liturgy (52:13–53:12) and Handel's Messiah, whose first part draws heavily on Isaiah. The seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' (6:3) is sung in the Sanctus of the Eucharist. Christian readers have also used the book against Jews, reading its judgments as aimed at them; this site presents Jewish readings beside Christian ones.

Isaiah supplies more prophetic readings (haftarot) in the synagogue than any other book. Above all, it gives the seven 'haftarot of consolation' read on the seven Sabbaths after the Ninth of Av, the fast for the destruction of the Temple: 40:1–26 (Shabbat Nachamu, 'Comfort'), 49:14–51:3, 54:11–55:5, 51:12–52:12, 54:1–10, 60:1–22 and 61:10–63:9. The Sabbath before the fast reads 1:1–27 (Shabbat Chazon, 'Vision'), and Yom Kippur morning reads 57:14–58:14, the true fast. The seraphim's song (6:3) is the heart of the Kedushah in every daily service.

The Targum of Isaiah, the Aramaic translation read in synagogues, gives the book a messianic reading in places such as 4:2, 9:6, 11:1, 42:1 and 52:13, while turning much of the suffering in chapter 53 onto Israel and the nations (Chilton). The medieval commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and David Kimchi read the servant of 40–55 mainly as the people of Israel, and Ibn Ezra hinted that the second half spoke from the time of the exile. Isaiah's hopes for a world at peace (2:4; 11:6–9) are central to Jewish teaching about the days of the Messiah.

sections.h: The death of Isaiah in later tradition
sections.b:
The Bible does not tell how Isaiah died. Jewish tradition held that King Manasseh, who 'shed a great deal of innocent blood' (2 Kings 21:16), had him killed. The Talmud tells that Manasseh charged Isaiah with contradicting Moses, since Isaiah claimed to have seen God (6:1; Exodus 33:20), and that Isaiah hid inside a cedar, which was then sawn in two (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b). The Martyrdom and Ascension of Isaiah, a Christian work of the first or second century AD with an older Jewish core, tells the same story of the saw and adds a vision of Isaiah's journey through the seven heavens (Knibb). The Lives of the Prophets says Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh and buried near the waters of Siloam. Most readers think Hebrews 11:37, 'they were sawn in two', alludes to this tradition, and Justin Martyr charged that the Jews had removed the story from the Scriptures (Dialogue with Trypho 120).

Sirach praises Isaiah as the prophet who strengthened Hezekiah and 'comforted the mourners in Zion' (Sirach 48:20–25). Josephus says that Cyrus read his own name in Isaiah's book, written long before, and was moved to let the Jews go home (Jewish Antiquities 11.5–6).

prompts:
The inside of a tall stone temple hall with great cedar doors whose stone sockets are shaking. High above, a throne on a raised platform, and from it the folds of a vast robe pour down and fill the whole floor of the hall. Above the throne hover winged figures, each with six wings: two covering its face, two covering its feet, two spread to fly, their bodies like flames. Smoke curls through the hall. Below, at the edge of the robe, a small man in a plain tunic falls back with his hand over his mouth.


Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

A high mountain rising above lower hills, with a simple temple on its summit. Long lines of people from many lands, in different dress, climb its paths like rivers flowing uphill. In the foreground a blacksmith at an anvil hammers a sword into the curved blade of a plow, while beside him another man bends a spearhead into a hooked pruning knife; a pile of broken shields lies at their feet.

An owner in a cloak stands at the gate holding a shriveled cluster in his open hand, looking at it.


Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. A wide desert of rocky hills and dry valleys at dawn. Through it workers are building a straight raised road: some fill a valley with stones, others level a hill with picks and baskets. Far down the road, toward the light on the horizon, a long line of people walk home carrying bundles and children. On a hilltop beside the road a lone figure with raised arms calls out.

traditions.q: Did Isaiah of Jerusalem write the whole book, or did later prophets write chapters 40–66?
views: In 1908 the Pontifical Biblical Commission ruled that the arguments for more than one author were not strong enough to set aside the tradition that Isaiah wrote the whole book. After Pius XII encouraged the study of the Bible's literary forms (Divino Afflante Spiritu, 1943), Catholic scholars came to accept widely that chapters 40–66 come from later prophets in Isaiah's tradition; the Church holds the whole book to be inspired Scripture, whoever its human authors were.

Divided. Many evangelical scholars, such as E. J. Young, Oswald Allis, Alec Motyer and John Oswalt, hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book, pointing to the book's claim to foretell (41:21–29; 46:9–10) and to the New Testament, which quotes both halves as Isaiah's (John 12:38–41). Others, such as John Goldingay, accept that chapters 40–66 address the exile from within it, and hold that this does not lessen their authority or inspiration.
